questions.stem: Which of the following structures is not found in prokaryotic cells?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.17): 'A prokaryotic cell lacks a true nucleus. The DNA … is coiled into a nucleoid region that is not surrounded by a membrane.'
Bacteria (prokaryotes) do have ribosomes, a cell wall, often a capsule, and pili/flagella (G9 pp.29–30). Answer: B.
tips: 'Pro-karyon' = before the nucleus: no membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is present in a bacterial cell?
explanation_steps: Ribosomes are not membrane-bound and occur in all cells, including bacteria. The others are membrane-bound organelles of eukaryotes. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The function of mitochondria is
explanation_steps: Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic cellular respiration: glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and respiration is 'completed in the mitochondria' (G10 p.117), releasing energy as ATP.
Protein transport = endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi; photosynthesis = chloroplasts; intracellular digestion = lysosomes; lipid synthesis = smooth ER. Answer: D.
tips: Mitochondria = 'powerhouse' of the cell (ATP production).

similar_questions.stem: Which organelle carries out intracellular digestion?
explanation_steps: Lysosomes contain digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Unlike animal cells, plant cells have ____, ____ and ____.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.15) lists the structures a plant cell has but an animal cell lacks: a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent (central) vacuole.
Mitochondria and nucleoplasm occur in both; centrioles and glycocalyx are animal-cell features. Answer: C.
tips: Plant-only trio: Wall, Chloroplasts, large central Vacuole.

similar_questions.stem: Which structure is found in animal cells but usually NOT in plant cells?
explanation_steps: Centrioles (used in animal cell division) are absent from most plant cells. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Diffusion does not require a cell to spend ATP. Therefore, diffusion is considered a type of
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.19): movement of substances across a membrane without the cell spending energy is called passive transport; diffusion and osmosis are examples.
Endocytosis, exocytosis, pinocytosis and active transport all use ATP. Answer: D.
tips: Down the concentration gradient = passive (no ATP); against it = active (ATP).

similar_questions.stem: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution is
explanation_steps: This is osmosis, a passive process (G9 p.21). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The branch of biology that studies about the formation and structure of a cell is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.3): 'Cytology – the study of the formation, structure, and function of cells.'
Morphology = form of organisms; microbiology = micro-organisms; parasitology = parasites; embryology = development of embryos. Answer: C.
tips: Cyto- = cell.

similar_questions.stem: The study of the development of an organism from the fertilized egg is
explanation_steps: Embryology studies embryos and their development. Answer: B.

questions.stem: ATP is
explanation_steps: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the immediate energy source of cells and carries energy from respiration to the reactions that need it (G9 p.131; G9 Exercise 3.2 asks exactly this).
All living organisms make ATP; aerobic respiration makes most of it (38 ATP per glucose, G9 p.131), though anaerobic respiration also makes a little.
Every statement is true. Answer: E.
tips: ATP = the cell's 'energy currency'.

similar_questions.stem: How many ATP molecules does the complete aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yield, according to the textbook?
explanation_steps: The textbook (G9 p.131) states that the energy of one glucose molecule can be used to make 38 ATP molecules in aerobic respiration.

questions.stem: What is the basic unit of a protein?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.7): 'amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.' Amino acids join by peptide bonds into polypeptides, which fold into proteins.
A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids, not the basic unit; fatty acids build lipids; glucose builds carbohydrates; enzymes are proteins. Answer: C.
tips: Monomers: glucose → carbohydrates; amino acids → proteins; fatty acids + glycerol → fats; nucleotides → nucleic acids.

similar_questions.stem: The bond that joins two amino acids is a
explanation_steps: Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds (–CO–NH–). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Through which path does blood typically flow in the circulatory system?
explanation_steps: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, divide into arterioles and then capillaries (where exchange happens); capillaries join into venules and veins, which return blood to the heart (G10 pp.61–64).
Answer: A.
tips: Heart → Artery → Arteriole → Capillary → Venule → Vein → Heart.

similar_questions.stem: The smallest blood vessels, which connect arterioles and venules, are
explanation_steps: Capillaries are the smallest vessels and connect arterioles to venules (G10 p.64). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which blood cells are the most numerous in the body?
explanation_steps: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are by far the most numerous blood cells – about 5 million per mm³ of blood, compared with about 7000 white cells and 250 000–400 000 platelets per mm³ (G10 p.67 onward).
Plasma is the liquid part of blood and capillaries are vessels, not cells. Answer: A.
tips: RBC ≫ platelets ≫ WBC in number.

similar_questions.stem: Which blood component is mainly responsible for clotting?
explanation_steps: Platelets (thrombocytes) start blood clotting. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Arteries branching away from the heart become smaller and smaller.
options.B: Veins leading back to the heart become smaller and smaller.
options.C: Arteries branching away from the heart become larger and larger.
options.D: Veins branching away from the heart become larger and larger.

explanation_steps: The aorta, the largest artery, branches into smaller arteries and finally fine arterioles (G10 p.61) – arteries get smaller away from the heart.
Veins do the opposite: venules merge into larger veins as they approach the heart, so B and C are false; D is meaningless (veins lead TOWARDS the heart). Answer: A.
tips: Arteries branch (get smaller) going out; veins merge (get larger) coming back.

similar_questions.stem: The largest artery in the body is the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.61): 'The aorta is the largest artery in the body.' Answer: B.

questions.stem: Compared to the walls of arteries, the walls of capillaries are
explanation_steps: Capillary walls are only one cell thick (an extension of the inner lining, G10 p.64), which allows exchange of materials; arteries have thick muscular, elastic walls.
C (lack valves) is also a true fact, but arteries lack valves too, so it is not a comparison with arteries; and 'lack valves' does not complete 'the walls … are' grammatically. Answer: A.
tips: Capillaries: one-cell-thick wall → easy diffusion.

similar_questions.stem: Which blood vessels contain valves to prevent back-flow of blood?
explanation_steps: Veins carry blood at low pressure and have valves. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a first line defense mechanism.
explanation_steps: The first line of defence keeps microbes out: the skin and mucous membranes, mucus and cilia, and chemical secretions such as tears and saliva (G10 p.101).
White blood cells (phagocytes, lymphocytes) attack microbes that have already entered the body – second/third lines of defence. Answer: C.
tips: 1st line = barriers (skin, mucus, cilia, secretions); 2nd = phagocytes, inflammation, fever; 3rd = specific immunity (antibodies).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following belongs to the specific (third-line) immune response?
explanation_steps: Antibodies produced by B-lymphocytes against a particular antigen are a specific response. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Mammalian skin plays a great role in
explanation_steps: Skin is a barrier against microbes (immunity, first line of defence, G10 p.101), excretes sweat containing water, salts and urea (G10 p.129), and is a sense organ for touch, pressure, heat, cold and pain (G10 p.143).
Option C is printed 'hemostasis' (stopping bleeding); this is almost certainly a typing error for 'homeostasis' – skin regulates body temperature by sweating and changes in blood flow (G11 p.95).
With C read as homeostasis, every option is a role of skin. Answer: E.
tips: Skin: protection, excretion, sensation, temperature regulation (homeostasis), vitamin D synthesis.

similar_questions.stem: Sweating helps to keep body temperature constant mainly because

options.B: evaporation of sweat absorbs heat from the skin

explanation_steps: Evaporation needs latent heat, which is taken from the skin and cools the body. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option C is printed 'hemostasis' (blood clotting); read as a typo for 'homeostasis' so that E is keyed. If read literally, skin has little role in haemostasis and no single option is fully correct – teacher to confirm E.

questions.stem: All of the following are functions of a kidney except
explanation_steps: The kidneys are the main excretory organs (remove urea and other wastes, G10 p.127) and osmoregulatory organs (control water and salt levels, G11 p.88). They also keep blood pH constant by excreting H⁺ ions and reabsorbing hydrogen-carbonate.
Since A–D are all kidney functions, there is no exception. Answer: E.
tips: 'Except … None of the above' = every listed item is true.

similar_questions.stem: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.134): 'The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the nephron.' Answer: B.

questions.stem: The hormone that is responsible for the regulation of metabolic processes is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.6): 'The chief functions of thyroxine are to control the body's metabolic rate…'
LH and FSH control reproduction, ADH controls water reabsorption, oxytocin causes uterine contraction and milk ejection. Answer: D.
tips: Thyroxine (needs iodine) = metabolic rate.

similar_questions.stem: Lack of iodine in the diet leads to enlargement of which gland?
explanation_steps: Without iodine, thyroxine cannot be made and the thyroid enlarges (goitre). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Estrogen and progesterone are produced by the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.12): the ovaries produce the female sex hormones oestrogen and progesterone (progesterone mainly by the corpus luteum).
Testes make testosterone; the adrenal glands make adrenaline and corticosteroids; the hypothalamus makes releasing hormones. Answer: C.
tips: Ovary → oestrogen + progesterone; testis → testosterone.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone is produced by the testes?
explanation_steps: The interstitial cells of the testes release androgens such as testosterone (G11 p.12). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Appendicular skeleton consists of the
explanation_steps: The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column and thorax (ribs and sternum); the appendicular skeleton is the limbs and their girdles (G11 p.63).
The femur (thigh bone) is a limb bone. Answer: A.
tips: Axial = axis of the body; Appendicular = appendages (arms, legs, girdles).

similar_questions.stem: Which bone belongs to the axial skeleton?
explanation_steps: Ribs are part of the thorax, which is axial. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Transcription is the

options.A: synthesis of another copy of a DNA molecule.
options.B: synthesis of messenger RNA, a complimentary copy of one strand of DNA.
options.C: synthesis of DNA, a complimentary copy of one strand of messenger RNA.
options.D: synthesis of transfer RNA from a molecule of messenger RNA.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.10): making an mRNA strand from DNA is called transcription; it is carried out by RNA polymerase, using one DNA strand as template, so the mRNA is complementary to it.
A describes replication; C describes reverse transcription; D is not a real process ('complimentary' in the options is a spelling error for 'complementary'). Answer: B.
tips: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.

similar_questions.stem: The process in which ribosomes use the code in mRNA to join amino acids into a protein is
explanation_steps: This is translation. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Bacteria are found everywhere except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.63): bacteria live 'in every place where life is possible, including hot springs, deep ocean beds, air, water, soil, and on surfaces of objects'.
All the places listed have bacteria. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Bacteria that live in very hot or very salty places belong to the group called
explanation_steps: Archaebacteria live in extreme environments such as hot springs and salt lakes. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about the members of the Kingdom Plantae?

options.B: Ferns, club mosses and horse tails have true roots, stems and leaves.
options.C: Gymnosperms are also known as naked-seed plants.
options.D: The common name of Angiosperms is flowering plants.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 pp.82–85): bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) have no vascular tissue; pteridophytes 'include ferns, club mosses, and horse tails. They have true roots, stems and leaves'; 'Gymnosperms are also known as naked-seed plants'; angiosperms are the flowering plants.
All four statements are correct. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: In which group of plants are the seeds enclosed in a fruit?
explanation_steps: Angiosperms (angio = vessel) have ovules inside an ovary, which becomes the fruit. Answer: D.

questions.stem: If Monera is to bacteria, ____ is to sponges.
explanation_steps: Bacteria belong to kingdom Monera. Sponges (phylum Porifera) are multicellular, heterotrophic animals without cell walls, so they belong to kingdom Animalia (five-kingdom system, G9 p.55).
Answer: B.
tips: Five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

similar_questions.stem: Amoeba and Paramecium belong to kingdom
explanation_steps: They are unicellular eukaryotes – protists. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following activities of an organism is not considered a mechanism of adaptation to environmental stress factors?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.141): adaptations to stress are 'classified as avoidance, tolerance and escape mechanisms'.
Digestion is an ordinary life process (breaking down food), not a response to stress. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A desert annual plant completes its life cycle quickly during the short rainy season and survives the dry season as seeds. This is an example of
explanation_steps: The plant 'escapes' the drought by not being active during it. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about adaptation?

options.A: It is the modification in structure or function that increases the fitness of an organism in a stressful environment.
options.B: It is hereditary and thus passed from one generation to the next.
options.C: It is a means of survival and without it species might become extinct.
options.D: It occurs as a result of an increase in those genes that allow individuals in a population to better survive and reproduce in a changing environment.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 pp.141–142): 'Adaptation is the modification in structure or function that increases the fitness…'; 'Adaptation is a means of survival and without it species might become extinct'; adaptations are inherited (G12 p.81) and spread because genes that help survival and reproduction increase in the population.
All statements are correct. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The thick fur of animals living in cold regions is best described as

options.D: a mutation that harms the animal

explanation_steps: Fur is a body structure that increases survival in the cold. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Carbohydrates are obtained from
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.3): carbohydrates are 'obtained from sugar cane, milk, bread, potatoes, wheat, pasta, cereals, injera and rice'. Milk contains the sugar lactose.
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The sugar found in milk is
explanation_steps: Milk sugar is lactose (glucose + galactose). Answer: C.

questions.stem: The following organs are part of the human digestive system except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.44): 'The human digestive system includes the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and …' – stomach, mouth, pharynx and oesophagus are all listed organs of the alimentary canal.
A tooth is a structure inside the mouth (an accessory part) and is not listed as a separate organ of the canal, so the intended answer is C.
Note: teeth do take part in digestion (mechanical breakdown), so the question is weak.
tips: Alimentary canal: mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the alimentary canal?
explanation_steps: The liver is an accessory gland: its bile enters the canal but food does not pass through it. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Teeth are part of the digestive system (mechanical digestion); C is keyed only because a tooth is a structure within the mouth rather than a separate organ of the canal. Teacher to confirm.

questions.stem: Which of the following body parts is without lymph nodes?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.90) lists the main groups of lymph nodes: cervical, axillary, inguinal, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, thoracic cavity and supratrochlear.
The brain and spinal cord (central nervous system) are not on the list; they have no lymph nodes. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Lymph nodes in the armpit belong to which region?
explanation_steps: Underarm (armpit) nodes are axillary nodes (G10 p.90). Answer: C.

questions.stem: In bread making, which is an example of alcohol fermentation, glucose is converted into

options.A: lactic acid, carbon dioxide and energy.
options.B: ethyl alcohol, carbon dioxide and water.
options.C: ethyl alcohol, carbon dioxide and energy.

explanation_steps: Alcohol fermentation by yeast (G10 pp.119–120): C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy (2 ATP). The CO₂ makes dough rise.
Water is not a product (B); lactic acid is the product of lactic acid fermentation in muscles (A, E); CO₂ + water + energy is aerobic respiration (D). Answer: C.
tips: Yeast: glucose → ethanol + CO₂ + energy. Muscle: glucose → lactic acid + energy.

similar_questions.stem: During strenuous exercise, human muscle cells short of oxygen convert glucose into
explanation_steps: This is lactic acid fermentation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about the retina?

options.A: Image of an object is formed on the retina.
options.B: Photoreceptor cells called rods and cones are present in the retina.
options.C: The rod cells are stimulated in bright light.
options.D: The cone cells are stimulated in dim light.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.152): 'The image of an object is formed on the retina. Photoreceptors (rod and cone cells) are present in the retina. Rod cells are stimulated in dim light… cone cells are stimulated only in bright light.'
So A and B are true, C and D are reversed. Answer: E.
tips: Rods = dim light (night vision); Cones = Colour, bright light.

similar_questions.stem: The part of the retina with no rods or cones, where the optic nerve leaves, is the
explanation_steps: The blind spot has no light-sensitive cells (G10 p.149). Answer: B.

questions.stem: A clump of neuron cell bodies is called a/an
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.167): 'A clump of neuron cell bodies is called a ganglion (plural: ganglia). A fibre made up of many axons is called a nerve.'
A synapse is a junction between neurons; an axon is one process of a neuron. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: The junction between two neurons is called a
explanation_steps: Signals pass from one neuron to the next at a synapse. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A tube that runs through the centre of the penis, through which semen and urine pass, is the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.30): the urethra is a 'tube running through the centre of the penis. Semen and urine passes through this structure.'
The vas deferens carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra; the scrotum holds the testes. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: The tube that carries sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra is the
explanation_steps: This is the vas deferens (sperm duct) (G11 p.30). Answer: B.

questions.stem: In females, the cells of the corpus luteum produce the hormone progesterone under the influence of
explanation_steps: LH from the anterior pituitary triggers ovulation and turns the empty follicle into the corpus luteum, which then produces progesterone (G11 pp.3, 33).
FSH stimulates follicle growth; GnRH acts on the pituitary, not the corpus luteum. Answer: B.
tips: FSH → follicle grows (oestrogen); LH → ovulation and corpus luteum (progesterone).

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone maintains the lining of the uterus after ovulation?
explanation_steps: Progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the endometrium thick (G11 p.33). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The absorption of water by seeds is called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.107): 'The absorption of water by seeds is called imbibition.' It activates the enzymes that start germination.
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants is called
explanation_steps: This is transpiration. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The nucleic acid that functions as a physical carrier of genetic information that passes from generation to generation is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.7; G9 p.126): DNA 'is a physical carrier of genetic information that passes from generation to generation.'
The RNAs help express the information (protein synthesis). Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome?
explanation_steps: Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about plant tissues?

options.A: Parenchyma tissues are the most abundant tissues, found in almost all major parts of higher plants.
options.B: Collenchyma tissues are found just beneath the epidermis and remain alive for a long period of time.
options.C: Sclerenchyma tissues are dead at maturity and provide only structure and support.
options.D: Some parenchyma cells have many chloroplasts and form the tissues found in leaves.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 pp.112–113): 'Parenchyma is the most abundant cell type, found in almost all major parts of higher plants'; parenchyma with many chloroplasts carries out photosynthesis in leaves; collenchyma cells have living protoplasm, lie just under the epidermis and give flexible support; 'At maturity, most sclerenchyma cells are dead and provide only structure and support.'
All four statements match the textbook. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which plant tissue has thick walls impregnated with lignin?
explanation_steps: Sclerenchyma cells have thick, lignified secondary walls. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about the nitrogenous bases of nucleic acids?

options.A: Adenine, uracil and cytosine are found in both DNA and RNA.
options.B: Adenine, uracil and cytosine are found only in DNA.
options.C: Adenine, uracil and cytosine are found in RNA.
options.D: Cytosine, thymine and adenine are found in RNA.
options.E: Thymine, guanine and cytosine are found in both DNA and RNA.

explanation_steps: DNA bases: A, T, G, C. RNA bases: A, U, G, C – RNA has uracil instead of thymine (G12 pp.3–5).
Uracil is not in DNA (A, B wrong); thymine is not in RNA (D, E wrong). Answer: C.
tips: T only in DNA, U only in RNA.

similar_questions.stem: How many hydrogen bonds join cytosine to guanine in DNA?
explanation_steps: Three hydrogen bonds join C and G; two join A and T (G12 p.4). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Chemistry has an application in

options.C: increasing the shelf life of food products.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 pp.2–3) lists applications of chemistry: medicines (antibiotics, pain killers, vaccines), disinfectants and germicides, building materials and plastics, food preservatives, and fertilisers and pesticides for agriculture.
Every option is an application. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Fertilisers such as urea and ammonium sulphate are products of the chemical industry that mainly help
explanation_steps: Fertilisers supply nitrogen to crops – an agricultural application. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following ionic compounds is useful in preventing the deficiency of iodine?
explanation_steps: Potassium iodide (KI) is added to table salt ('iodized salt') to supply iodine and prevent goitre (textbook G9 p.67 list of ionic compounds and their uses).
Mg(OH)₂ is an antacid, NaF prevents tooth decay, KCl is a fertiliser/salt substitute, NaCl is common salt. Answer: D.
tips: Iodine → thyroxine → prevents goitre (links to biology Q15).

similar_questions.stem: Which compound is added to toothpaste to prevent tooth decay?
explanation_steps: Fluoride (sodium fluoride) strengthens tooth enamel. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The chemical symbol for cobalt is
explanation_steps: A two-letter symbol has a capital first letter and a small second letter (G9 p.80). Cobalt = Co.
CO (capital O) is the compound carbon monoxide; Cl = chlorine; Ca = calcium; Cb is not a current symbol. Answer: B.
tips: Capital + small letter: Co (cobalt) ≠ CO (carbon monoxide).

similar_questions.stem: Which symbol represents copper?
explanation_steps: Copper = Cu (from Latin cuprum). Answer: C.

questions.stem: In the periodic table, the group VIIIA is known as
explanation_steps: Group VIIIA (group 18) contains He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn – the noble gases (formerly inert gases) (G10 p.15).
IA = alkali metals, IIA = alkaline-earth metals, IVA = carbon family, VIIA = halogens; transition metals are the B groups. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine belong to group
explanation_steps: They are the halogens, group VIIA. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about a covalent bond?

options.A: It involves the transfer of electrons.
options.B: It deals with the sharing of electrons.
options.C: It takes place between metals and nonmetals.
options.D: MgO is formed by a covalent bond.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.43): 'A covalent bond is formed by two nonmetallic atoms when they share' valence electrons.
Transfer of electrons between a metal and a non-metal forms an ionic bond; MgO is ionic (Mg²⁺O²⁻). Answer: B.
tips: Ionic = transfer (metal + non-metal); covalent = sharing (non-metal + non-metal).

similar_questions.stem: Which compound contains covalent bonds?
explanation_steps: Carbon and hydrogen are both non-metals and share electrons. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a heterogeneous mixture?
explanation_steps: A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform and has more than one phase (G9 p.25). Oil does not dissolve in water, so two layers form.
Salt water, ethanol–water, air and sugar water are uniform solutions (homogeneous). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture?
explanation_steps: Air is a uniform mixture of gases. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following solutions is an acid.
explanation_steps: Gastric juice in the stomach contains hydrochloric acid (G10 p.125).
Milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂), ammonium hydroxide and household ammonia are bases; brine (NaCl solution) is neutral. Answer: E.

questions.stem: The image formed on the screen of a pinhole camera is
explanation_steps: Light travels in straight lines through the pinhole, so rays from the top of the object reach the bottom of the screen: the image is real (it forms on a screen) and inverted (G10 pp.213–215).

For a normal camera the object is much farther from the hole than the screen, so the image is diminished. (Strictly, image height/object height = image distance/object distance, so it could be magnified if the screen were farther than the object; B is the usual case.) Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: A pinhole camera 20 cm long views a tree 30 m away that is 6 m tall. How tall is the image?
explanation_steps: image height/object height = image distance/object distance → image height = 6 × 0.20/30 = 0.04 m = 4 cm (real, inverted).

questions.stem: When an object is beyond the centre of curvature of a converging mirror, the image is formed

options.A: at the focus of the mirror.
options.B: between the focus and centre of curvature of the mirror.
options.C: between the pole and focus of the mirror.
options.D: at the centre of curvature of the mirror.

explanation_steps: For a concave (converging) mirror, an object beyond C gives a real, inverted, diminished image between F and C (G10 p.239 table).
Object at infinity → image at F; object at C → image at C; object at F → image at infinity. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: An object is 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image?
similar_questions.answer: 15 cm in front of the mirror
explanation_steps: 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/d₀ = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30 → dᵢ = 15 cm (between F = 10 cm and C = 20 cm).

questions.stem: A lens has a power of +2.50 D. The radius of curvature of the lens is
explanation_steps: Power P = 1/f (f in metres) (G11 p.33): f = 1/2.50 = 0.40 m = 40 cm (converging lens).
The textbook relation R = 2f is given only for spherical mirrors (G10 p.231); applying it here gives R = 2 × 40 = 80 cm – almost certainly the examiner's intended answer (A).

Physically, a thin lens obeys the lens-maker's formula 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂). For a symmetric (equiconvex) glass lens with n = 1.5, 1/f = 0.5 × 2/R = 1/R, so R = f = 40 cm (C). Because the question gives neither n nor the lens shape, both A and C are accepted.
tips: Power in dioptres = 1/(focal length in metres).

questions.stem: In a compound microscope the

options.A: focal length of the eyepiece is smaller than the focal length of the objective lens.
options.B: first image produced by the objective lens is real, magnified and erect.
options.C: final image of a very small object is virtual, magnified and inverted.
options.D: final image is produced by the objective lens.
options.E: first image of a very small object is produced by reflection.

explanation_steps: A compound microscope has two converging lenses (G11 pp.36–37). The objective (very short focal length) forms a real, magnified, INVERTED first image; the eyepiece (longer focal length) acts as a magnifying glass on it and forms the final virtual, magnified image, which is still inverted relative to the object.
A reverses the focal lengths; B is wrong (the first image is inverted); D is wrong (the eyepiece forms the final image); E is wrong (lenses refract). Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: In a compound microscope, the objective magnifies 10× and the eyepiece 5×. What is the total magnification?
explanation_steps: Total magnification = m(objective) × m(eyepiece) = 10 × 5 = 50.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about a transformer?

options.A: The primary and the secondary coils are wound on a laminated core of soft iron.
options.B: A transformer operates only on AC.
options.C: The primary coil is connected to a source of AC voltage and emf is induced in the secondary coil.
options.D: The voltage induced in the secondary coil is proportional to the primary voltage and turn ratio.
options.E: A transformer steps up or steps down the electrical power.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 pp.132–134): the primary and secondary coils 'are wound on a laminated core of magnetically soft material'; an alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux that induces an emf in the secondary; it therefore works only with AC; Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ, i.e. Vₛ = Vₚ × (Nₛ/Nₚ).
So A, B, C and D are all true. Only E is false: a transformer steps voltage up or down, but it cannot increase power (ideally Pₛ = Pₚ; in practice Pₛ < Pₚ).
The item has four correct options; C (the basic principle of operation) is keyed and A, B and D are also accepted. The examiner may have meant 'Which statement is NOT true?', whose answer would be E.
tips: Transformers change voltage and current, never (increase) power.

similar_questions.stem: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 1000 turns on the secondary. If the primary voltage is 12 V AC, what is the secondary voltage?
explanation_steps: Vₛ = Vₚ × Nₛ/Nₚ = 12 × 1000/200 = 60 V (step-up).

questions.review_flag: Four options (A–D) are true and only E is false; the stem may have intended 'not true' (answer E). A–D accepted, C keyed; teacher to decide.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is wrong about a magnet?

options.A: It attracts all metals and their alloys.
options.B: It exerts force on other magnets and magnetic materials.
options.D: It may have different size and shape.
options.E: It has important application in electrical appliances.

explanation_steps: A magnet attracts only magnetic (ferromagnetic) materials such as iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their alloys (G11 pp.65–70). Copper, aluminium, gold, brass, etc. are not attracted.
B–E are true: magnets always have two poles, come in bar, horseshoe, ring and other shapes, and are used in motors, loudspeakers and generators. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which material is attracted by a magnet?
explanation_steps: Nickel is ferromagnetic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about a mechanical wave?

options.A: It is a repeating disturbance that travels through a medium.
options.B: It is produced by a vibrating body.
options.D: It does not propagate through empty space.
options.E: It transports matter from one region to another in space.

explanation_steps: A mechanical wave is a disturbance (produced by a vibrating source) that travels through a material medium and carries energy, but the particles of the medium only vibrate about their fixed positions – no matter is carried along (G11 pp.146–148). It cannot travel through a vacuum.
Answer: E.
tips: Waves carry energy, not matter.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following waves can travel through a vacuum?
explanation_steps: Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The energy of a single photon of light is 2.35 eV. The wavelength of the light is [h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J]
explanation_steps: E = hc/λ (G12 p.101) → λ = hc/E.
tips: Shortcut: λ(nm) ≈ 1243/E(eV) with these constants.

questions.stem: Refraction of waves is accompanied by a change in

options.A: the speed and wavelength of the wave.
options.B: the speed and frequency of the wave.
options.C: frequency and wavelength of the wave.
options.D: frequency and period of the wave.
options.E: frequency, wavelength and period of the wave.

explanation_steps: When a wave enters a new medium its frequency (and so its period) is fixed by the source and does not change; its speed changes, so its wavelength (λ = v/f) changes too (G11 pp.168–169).
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass in which its speed is 2 × 10⁸ m/s. What is its wavelength in the glass? [c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s]
explanation_steps: Frequency is unchanged, so λ(glass) = λ(air) × v(glass)/c = 600 × 2/3 = 400 nm.

questions.stem: The pressure at a point in a liquid

options.B: decreases with depth in the liquid.
options.C: increases with elevation in the liquid.

explanation_steps: Liquid pressure at a point acts equally in all directions and increases with depth: p = ρgh (G12 pp.15–17).
Answer: D.

questions.stem: A liquid of mass 2000 g completely fills a 0.5 litre container. The relative density of the liquid is
explanation_steps: Density = m/V = 2000 g / 500 cm³ = 4.0 g/cm³.
Relative density = density of liquid / density of water (1.0 g/cm³) = 4.0 (G12 pp.4–6). Answer: A.
tips: Relative density has no unit.

similar_questions.stem: A 250 cm³ bottle holds 200 g of oil. What is the relative density of the oil?

questions.stem: In a tube resting vertically, a column of water 56 cm high supports a column of an unknown liquid of relative density 1.6. The height of the column of the unknown liquid is
explanation_steps: The two columns exert equal pressures (U-tube, G12 p.27): ρ(water) g h(water) = ρ(liquid) g h(liquid).
h(liquid) = h(water) × ρ(water)/ρ(liquid) = 56 × 1/1.6 = 35 cm. Answer: D. (The denser liquid stands lower.)

questions.stem: The shortest wavelength present in the radiation from an x-ray machine whose accelerating potential is 50 000 V is [h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C]
